title: The singular after the plural in Hosea is deliberate, as Genesis shows
english: After reading, “They wept and begged me,” and, “Being in the house, they found me,” someone might say that what follows is also, “There it was spoken to them.” That is, to those who wept and begged, and who, being in the house, found God. And from observation of similar sayings we will show that this too has been said consistently.

In Genesis, when God gives a command to Adam, God speaks like this: “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die” (Genesis 2:16-17). For there too, having begun from the singular in saying, “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food,” God brings in the plural, saying, “But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die” (Genesis 2:17). For when it concerns the command through which God willed Adam to be in life by keeping it, he commands in the singular, and says, “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food” (Genesis 2:16).

title: The many who walk with God are one
english: Those who walk according to God and hold fast to his commandments, even if they are many, are one by being of one mind. For this reason, when a command about something good is given, it is said in the singular: “You shall eat for food” (Genesis 2:16). But when the matter of transgression is already being distinguished, he no longer speaks in the singular but in the plural: “You shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat, by death you shall die” (Genesis 2:17).

So here too, while they are still weeping and beseeching God, it is said in the plural: “They wept and beseeched” (Hosea 12:4). But when they find God, he no longer says in the plural, “There it was spoken to them,” but “to him” (Hosea 12:4). For the many have already become one in having found God and in hearing his word.

title: The one who sins becomes many; the many who obey become one
english: For the one who sins becomes many, because he is split off from God and divided, and he falls out of the unity. But the many who follow the commandments of God are one. The Apostle testifies to this when he says: “Because we, the many, are one bread and one body”. And again: “One God, and one Christ, and one faith, and one baptism”. And elsewhere: “Because we are all one in Christ Jesus”. And again: “For I betrothed you all to one husband, a pure virgin, to present to the Lord”.

And that those who please the Lord are one can be seen from the prayer that the Savior prays to the Father for his disciples. “Holy Father,” he says, “grant that just as I and you are one, so also these may be one in us.” And when the saints are said to be members of one another, what else are they but one body? And in the Shepherd of Hermas, when the building of the tower is built from many stones but the building appears to be from one stone, what else does Scripture signify but the harmony and unity that comes from many?
